script.opening: "Hi, I'm really worried. My right hand keeps going numb and tingly, especially at night — it wakes me up and I have to shake it to get the feeling back. I've been dropping things too. I looked it up and now I'm petrified it's the start of MS, or that I'm heading for a stroke. My hand going numb has to mean something's wrong with my nerves or brain, doesn't it?"

facts.text: Thumb, index and middle finger of the right hand, and "maybe half the ring finger". The little finger is fine.

About six weeks. Wakes you two or three times a night; you hang your hand over the side of the bed and shake it and the feeling comes back in a few minutes. Also when holding the phone or driving. Daytime it is mostly fine.
Dropping cups, fumbling with buttons. If asked whether the muscle at the base of your thumb looks thinner: "I don't think so — they look the same."

Left hand fine. No neck pain. No numbness or weakness in the legs, face or anywhere else. No problems with speech, vision, balance, bladder or bowels. Nothing came on suddenly. Never had episodes like this before.

Put on about a stone this year, always tired, "always cold — I wear a cardigan when everyone else is in T-shirts", skin dry. Periods irregular lately. Not pregnant (you had a test because of the irregular periods — negative). Not thirsty, not passing more urine.
Nothing significant. No regular medicines. No allergies.
48, works on the checkout at a supermarket — scanning all day. Married, two grown-up children. Non-smoker.
A woman at work, Julie, was diagnosed with MS last year "and it started with numbness". Say this only if asked what made you think of MS.

Anxious and fixed on MS or stroke. If the doctor just says "it's carpal tunnel, don't worry", stay unconvinced: "But how do you know it's not MS?" If they explain WHY the pattern fits a trapped nerve at the wrist and not MS or stroke, visibly relax. Be interested in the thyroid link: "I have been feeling rubbish."

ice.ideas: "Numbness means something wrong with my nerves or brain — MS or a stroke."
ice.concerns: "I'm scared I'll end up like Julie at work."
ice.expectations: To be told honestly whether it is MS or a stroke, and to get your sleep back.

cues: "I have to shake it to get the feeling back." — say in the opening.
"I'm petrified it's the start of MS." — say in the opening.
"I'm always cold these days." — say if asked about general health.

checkpoints.text: Recognises CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME from the classic history (median-nerve distribution tingling/numbness, worst at night, relieved by shaking the hand, clumsiness) and makes a confident POSITIVE diagnosis rather than an open-ended "could be anything"

Gives REASONED reassurance that distinguishes it from MS and stroke: the nocturnal, hand-specific, median pattern is the picture of a trapped nerve at the wrist — NOT the diffuse/relapsing CNS pattern of MS nor the sudden focal deficit of a stroke — explaining WHY, not just saying "it’s nothing"

Screens for treatable ASSOCIATIONS: hypothyroidism (her weight gain/tiredness/cold — check TFTs), diabetes (HbA1c), and considers pregnancy, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis and occupational/repetitive use — recognising the hand symptom can flag an underlying condition

Offers the MANAGEMENT ladder: nocturnal wrist splints first-line, activity/ergonomic modification and treating associations; corticosteroid injection; and referral for nerve conduction studies/decompression if severe, persistent, or motor signs (thenar wasting)

Knows the genuine red flags that would change the picture (bilateral/diffuse symptoms, CNS signs, sudden focal deficit, rapidly progressive weakness/wasting) and safety-nets for them — so reassurance is safe

Identifies the MS/stroke fear as the REAL reason for the call and addresses it directly and warmly (exploring any specific trigger), treating reassurance as a skilled, specific task rather than a brush-off
Validates the worry and the impact (sleep, dropping things, work) and engages her in the plan, so she feels heard and reassured

Safety-nets and follows up: the splint/management plan and association screening (TFTs/HbA1c), what new symptoms would warrant review (spreading/diffuse symptoms, weakness/wasting, CNS features), referral criteria, and a follow-up — confident diagnosis, treatable associations checked, fear resolved

worked.txt: "Let me start with the answer, because I can hear how frightened you are: what you’re describing is a classic picture of carpal tunnel syndrome — a nerve that gets squeezed where it passes through the wrist. The tingling in your thumb and first two fingers, worse at night, waking you, eased by shaking your hand — that’s textbook. I’m not guessing or being kind; the pattern really fits it."

"And here’s why it’s NOT the things you’ve been dreading. MS and strokes don’t behave like this — a trapped wrist nerve gives exactly this hand-only, night-time, shake-it-better pattern. MS tends to cause different, spreading symptoms over time, and a stroke comes on suddenly and affects more than a few fingers. Your story points firmly at the wrist, not the brain. That’s genuinely reassuring, and I can explain it because it’s true."

"Can I ask what set off the MS worry — did you read it, or does someone you know have it? … That makes sense. It’s natural your mind went there. But this really is a different, much more ordinary and treatable thing."

"A couple of useful questions — have you gained weight, felt more tired or cold lately? … You have. Carpal tunnel can be linked to an underactive thyroid, and to diabetes, so I’d like to do a couple of blood tests — partly because treating those can help the hand too. The hand can be the first clue to something simple and fixable."

"For the hand itself: the first and often very effective step is a wrist splint worn at night to keep the wrist straight — that alone settles a lot of people. We can also look at how you’re using your wrist at work. If it doesn’t settle, there’s a steroid injection, and for stubborn cases nerve tests and a small operation that cures it. So there’s a clear path, and it works."

"Now, so you know when to come back rather than worry: if the numbness spreads beyond the hand, you get weakness or wasting at the base of the thumb, or anything sudden affecting your face, speech or other limbs — tell us, as that’d need a different look. But what you’ve described is the ordinary, treatable kind. Splint at night, I’ll do those bloods, and we’ll review. You rang terrified it was your brain; it’s your wrist, and we can fix it."

f.learning: Tingling/numbness in the MEDIAN nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, half ring finger), worst AT NIGHT, waking the patient and relieved by shaking the hand, with clumsiness, is classic CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME — a benign median-nerve compression at the wrist — and warrants a confident POSITIVE diagnosis. The examinable communication task is REASONED reassurance that distinguishes it from the patient’s googled fears: the nocturnal, hand-specific, median pattern is NOT the diffuse/relapsing CNS pattern of MS nor the sudden focal deficit of a stroke — explained, not dismissed ("it’s just carpal tunnel" without the why will fail). Screen for treatable ASSOCIATIONS (hypothyroidism — her weight gain/tiredness/cold — diabetes, pregnancy, obesity, RA, occupational use), since the hand symptom can flag an underlying condition. Offer the management ladder (nocturnal wrist splints first, ergonomic modification and treating associations; steroid injection; nerve conduction studies/decompression for severe/persistent/motor signs), and safety-net the genuine red flags (diffuse/bilateral symptoms, CNS signs, sudden focal deficit, progressive wasting) so reassurance is safe.

knowledge.guideline: BSSH/GIRFT carpal tunnel pathway (2022) · NICE NG127 · NICE NG145 · NICE NG220
knowledge.summary: Night-time tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking the hand, is carpal tunnel syndrome. Make a confident diagnosis, explain why it is not MS or stroke, screen for associations, and start with a night splint.

points.t: Paraesthesia or numbness in the median nerve territory (thumb, index, middle and the radial half of the ring finger), worse at night and waking the patient, relieved by shaking the hand. Clumsiness and dropping things are common. Phalen’s and Tinel’s tests support the diagnosis, which is clinical.

points.h: Why it isn’t MS or stroke
points.t: Stroke causes sudden weakness or numbness, usually of the face, arm or leg, not intermittent tingling in three fingers at night. MS typically causes episodes lasting days to weeks, often with vision, balance or bladder symptoms (NICE NG220). A median-territory, positional, nocturnal pattern points to the wrist.
Hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly and repetitive wrist use. Her weight gain, tiredness and cold intolerance justify TSH (NICE NG145). Check HbA1c as well.

Constant numbness, weak thumb abduction or thenar wasting mean significant compression. These need prompt referral for surgery rather than more splinting (BSSH/GIRFT 2022). Arrange a face-to-face check of the thenar muscles if she is dropping things.

BSSH/GIRFT 2022: a neutral-position wrist splint worn at night, and changes to aggravating activity, first. Then a corticosteroid injection. Then referral for nerve conduction studies and carpal tunnel release if symptoms persist or are severe. Treat any underlying cause.

Symptoms in both hands and feet, spreading beyond the median territory, neck pain with arm symptoms, or other neurological signs suggest a different diagnosis. NICE NG127 covers referral of suspected neurological conditions.

Confident, positive diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome, with the reasoning shared.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

model.text: Hello, is that Donna? … Thanks for calling. I understand you’re worried about your hand. Tell me what’s been happening.

I’m really worried. My right hand keeps going numb and tingly, especially at night. It wakes me up and I have to shake it. I’ve been dropping things too. I looked it up and now I’m petrified it’s MS, or that I’m heading for a stroke.
That sounds frightening, and I’m glad you rang. I’d like to ask some specific questions, because the details really matter, and then I’ll tell you honestly what I think. Is that OK?
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
Which fingers are affected — all of them, or some more than others?
The thumb, first finger and middle finger mostly. Not the little finger.
And is it there all the time, or does it come and go? What brings it on?
Mostly at night, and sometimes at work when I’m scanning at the till for hours. It goes if I shake my hand.
When you drop things, is the hand weak, or is it more that you can’t feel what you’re holding? Have you noticed the fleshy part at the base of your thumb looking thinner?
model.why: Screens for motor involvement and wasting

model.text: More that my fingers feel clumsy. I haven’t looked at my thumb, to be honest.
Any symptoms in the other hand, your feet, or your face? Any problems with your vision, balance, speech, or your bladder?
model.why: Screens for CNS and polyneuropathy features

model.text: No. Just this hand.
Any neck pain or pain going down the arm?
No, nothing like that.
A few general questions too. How have you been in yourself — energy, weight, feeling the cold?
Funny you ask. I’ve put on weight, I’m shattered, and I’m always cold. I thought it was my age.
That’s helpful. You mentioned MS and stroke. What have you read that’s made you think of those?
It said numbness and tingling can be the first sign of MS. And a numb hand can be a stroke. I haven’t slept properly for a week.
That sounds really hard — lying awake worrying on top of being woken by your hand. What were you hoping I could do today?
model.why: Validates the impact and elicits expectations

model.text: Just tell me if it’s one of those. And stop it waking me up.

Then let me give you the answer first. What you’re describing is a very typical picture of carpal tunnel syndrome. That’s a nerve being squeezed as it passes through a tunnel at the front of your wrist. The thumb and first two fingers, worse at night, better when you shake your hand — that’s exactly the nerve’s territory.
So it’s not my brain?

Everything you’ve told me points to the wrist, not the brain. A stroke comes on suddenly and usually affects the face, arm or leg, and it doesn’t come and go with shaking your hand. MS tends to cause symptoms that last days or weeks, often with eyesight or balance problems. You don’t have any of those. I’m saying this because the pattern fits, not just to reassure you.
model.why: Reasoned explanation of why it is not MS or stroke

model.text: (breathes out) Oh. OK. That’s such a relief.

I’m glad. The weight gain, tiredness and feeling cold could be an underactive thyroid, which can cause carpal tunnel. I’d like a blood test for your thyroid, and for sugar, because diabetes is another link. If the thyroid is low, treating it can help the hand too.
That would explain a lot.

For the hand itself, the first step is a wrist splint worn at night, which keeps the wrist straight and takes pressure off the nerve. It helps a lot of people. It’s also worth looking at how you use your wrist at the till: short breaks, and keeping your wrist straight if you can.
I can do that. Will I need an operation?

Most people don’t. If the splint isn’t enough, a steroid injection often helps. If it still doesn’t settle, or the nerve is being damaged, a nerve test and a small operation usually cure it. Because you’re dropping things, I’d like to see you in person to check the strength and muscles at the base of your thumb — can you come in this week?
model.why: Management ladder and in-person check for motor signs

model.text: Yes, I can come in on Thursday.
That works. Can I check one thing — would it help to have a note for work about adjusting your tasks while this settles?
Maybe. I’ll see how the splint goes.

That’s fine. So you know when to act: if you ever get sudden weakness or numbness of your face, arm or leg, slurred speech, or loss of vision, call 999. If the numbness spreads to your other hand or your feet, becomes constant, or your thumb gets weaker, let us know sooner.
model.why: Specific safety-net covering stroke and progression

model.text: OK.
Just so I know I’ve explained it clearly, what will you tell your family about what’s causing this?
That it’s a squashed nerve in my wrist, not MS or a stroke. Splint at night, blood test for my thyroid, and you’re checking my thumb on Thursday.
Exactly right. You rang frightened it was your brain; it’s your wrist, and it’s very treatable. See you on Thursday.
model.why: Summarises and closes on the reframe

social.t: Hours of scanning at the till may aggravate symptoms. Suggest breaks, wrist posture and task rotation. Occupational health, if her employer has one, can help.
Broken sleep from the hand plus a week of worry after searching online. Reasoned reassurance and a clear plan help both.

legal.t: If needed, a fit note can say ‘may be fit for work’ with suggested adjustments, such as reduced scanning time or task rotation, rather than time off.
Employers must report carpal tunnel syndrome under RIDDOR 2013 only when the work involves regular use of percussive or vibrating tools. Till scanning does not meet this.

professional.t: Telephone assessment can establish the diagnosis but not thenar wasting or weakness. Arrange a face-to-face examination when motor symptoms are reported, and document the reasoning.
Referring a classic history to neurology reinforces anxiety and uses scarce resources. Explain the diagnosis and the triggers for rethinking.

community.t: Many areas offer direct access to MSK physiotherapy or hand therapy for splints. The British Society for Surgery of the Hand has patient information on carpal tunnel syndrome.

redFlags: Sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, speech or vision loss — stroke; 999
Thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction or constant numbness — prompt surgical referral
Bilateral hand and foot symptoms, neck pain with arm symptoms, or other neurological signs — rethink the diagnosis
psychosocial: Hours of till scanning at work
Broken sleep and a week of worry after searching online
Weight gain, tiredness and feeling cold, put down to age
ice: Idea: “Numbness means MS or a stroke.”
Concern: a serious brain or nerve illness
Expectation: to be told whether it’s MS or a stroke, and to stop being woken at night

playbook.diagnosis: Give the answer first: “This is a typical picture of carpal tunnel syndrome — a nerve squeezed at the wrist. The fingers affected, the night-time pattern and the relief from shaking all point to the wrist, not the brain.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The nerve to your thumb and first fingers runs through a narrow tunnel at the wrist. At night, when your wrist bends, the tunnel narrows and squeezes the nerve — like standing on a hosepipe. Shaking your hand takes your foot off the pipe.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been lying awake thinking this was MS or a stroke. Everything you’ve described points to your wrist instead, and that’s very treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Address the fear directly, with reasons. Offer practical changes for till work and a fit note with adjustments if needed.
sharedPlan: Neutral-position night splint and activity changes (BSSH/GIRFT 2022)
TSH and HbA1c for associations (NICE NG145)
Face-to-face check of thenar bulk and thumb strength; injection, then nerve studies and surgery if persistent or motor signs
safetyNet: 999 for sudden face, arm or leg weakness or numbness, speech or vision loss
Review sooner if numbness spreads, becomes constant, or thumb weakness develops

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by vague or reasonless reassurance, missing the thyroid cue, or ignoring the limits of a telephone consultation. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: ‘It could be a few things — let’s do some tests and see.’
items.why: A classic history deserves a confident, positive diagnosis. Vagueness feeds her fear of MS.
items.fix: “This is a typical picture of carpal tunnel syndrome, and here’s why.”

items.fail: ‘It’s definitely not MS, don’t worry’ — with no explanation.
items.why: Unexplained reassurance doesn’t work with health anxiety. The fear is the reason for the call.
items.fix: Explain the difference: “Stroke is sudden and affects the face, arm or leg; MS lasts days to weeks with other symptoms. Yours follows one nerve at the wrist.”

items.fail: Missing the weight gain, tiredness and cold intolerance.
items.why: Hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of carpal tunnel syndrome (NICE NG145 for testing).
items.fix: Ask about general health and check TSH and HbA1c.

items.why: Thenar wasting or weakness means nerve damage and changes the plan to prompt surgical referral (BSSH/GIRFT 2022).
items.fix: “Because you’re dropping things, I’d like to check your thumb muscles in person this week.”

items.fail: Referring straight to neurology or for nerve conduction studies ‘to be safe’.
items.why: A typical history doesn’t need a nerve study before a splint. Referral reinforces the fear.
items.fix: Start with a night splint, and name exactly what would change the plan.

items.fail: No stroke safety-net because ‘it isn’t a stroke’.
items.why: She fears stroke. Telling her exactly what stroke looks like is both safe and reassuring.
items.fix: “Sudden weakness of your face, arm or leg, slurred speech or loss of vision — call 999. That’s different from what you have.”

timeMap.d: She leads with the MS and stroke fear. Acknowledge it and promise an honest answer after a few questions.
Which fingers, timing, shaking relief, weakness or wasting, other limbs, face, vision, balance, bladder, neck. Thyroid symptoms. Explore where the fear came from.
Name carpal tunnel confidently. Explain why the pattern is the wrist, not the brain.
Night splint, activity changes at the till, TSH and HbA1c, in-person thenar check because she is dropping things. Outline injection and surgery.
999 for stroke symptoms. Review sooner for spreading or constant numbness or weakness. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Says ‘it’s nothing to worry about’ without explaining why; or keeps the diagnosis vague and suggests a neurology referral; never asks about thyroid symptoms; no plan to check for weakness or wasting; no stroke safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises carpal tunnel, reassures that it isn’t MS or stroke, recommends a splint and checks thyroid function, basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: gives the answer early and explains the reasoning in plain language; explores where the fear came from; recognises that a phone call can’t assess thenar wasting and books a face-to-face check; addresses her till work; clear, specific safety-net; teach-back confirms relief and understanding.

avoid.instead: “Your symptoms follow one nerve at the wrist, come and go at night and ease with shaking — MS and stroke don’t behave like that.”
avoid.why: Reassurance without reasons doesn’t land with an anxious patient.

avoid.dont: “I’ll refer you to neurology to be on the safe side.”
avoid.instead: “This is a clear picture of carpal tunnel. Let’s start treatment, and I’ll tell you exactly what would make me think again.”
avoid.why: An unnecessary referral reinforces the fear and delays effective treatment.

avoid.instead: “Tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold can be an underactive thyroid, which can also cause this. Let’s check.”
avoid.why: Dismissing the cue misses a treatable association.

Exactly right. You rang frightened it was your brain; it’s your wrist, and it’s very treatable. See you on Thursday.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises and closes on the reframe

SCA_STEM.name: Donna Whitfield
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Several weeks of tingling and numbness in the right hand, worse at night. Works in a supermarket.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone consultation. Worried her hand symptoms mean multiple sclerosis or a stroke.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BSSH/GIRFT carpal tunnel pathway (2022) · NICE NG127 · NICE NG145 · NICE NG220
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Night-time tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking the hand, is carpal tunnel syndrome. Make a confident diagnosis, explain why it is not MS or stroke, screen for associations, and start with a night splint.

points.t: Paraesthesia or numbness in the median nerve territory (thumb, index, middle and the radial half of the ring finger), worse at night and waking the patient, relieved by shaking the hand. Clumsiness and dropping things are common. Phalen’s and Tinel’s tests support the diagnosis, which is clinical.

points.h: Why it isn’t MS or stroke
points.t: Stroke causes sudden weakness or numbness, usually of the face, arm or leg, not intermittent tingling in three fingers at night. MS typically causes episodes lasting days to weeks, often with vision, balance or bladder symptoms (NICE NG220). A median-territory, positional, nocturnal pattern points to the wrist.
Hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, obesity, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly and repetitive wrist use. Her weight gain, tiredness and cold intolerance justify TSH (NICE NG145). Check HbA1c as well.

Constant numbness, weak thumb abduction or thenar wasting mean significant compression. These need prompt referral for surgery rather than more splinting (BSSH/GIRFT 2022). Arrange a face-to-face check of the thenar muscles if she is dropping things.

BSSH/GIRFT 2022: a neutral-position wrist splint worn at night, and changes to aggravating activity, first. Then a corticosteroid injection. Then referral for nerve conduction studies and carpal tunnel release if symptoms persist or are severe. Treat any underlying cause.

Symptoms in both hands and feet, spreading beyond the median territory, neck pain with arm symptoms, or other neurological signs suggest a different diagnosis. NICE NG127 covers referral of suspected neurological conditions.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question on the telephone; let her voice the MS and stroke fear in full.
Supermarket till work, broken sleep, a week of worry after reading online.
Picked up the fear, ‘dropping things’ and the weight gain, tiredness and cold intolerance, and explored each.
Idea (MS or stroke); concern (a serious brain or nerve illness); expectation (an answer, and to stop being woken).
Finger territory, timing, relief by shaking; CNS and bilateral symptoms; face-to-face check of thenar bulk and thumb abduction; TSH and HbA1c.
Carpal tunnel syndrome versus cervical radiculopathy, peripheral neuropathy, MS and stroke.
Screened for CNS features, bilateral or spreading symptoms, neck pain and wasting; safety-netted stroke symptoms explicitly.
Confident, positive diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome, with the reasoning shared.
Night splint and activity changes first (BSSH/GIRFT 2022); injection next; referral for nerve studies and surgery if persistent, severe or motor signs.
TSH for possible hypothyroidism, HbA1c for diabetes; work adjustments offered.
999 for sudden face, arm or leg weakness, speech or vision loss; review sooner for spreading or constant numbness or thumb weakness; in-person check booked.

social.t: Hours of scanning at the till may aggravate symptoms. Suggest breaks, wrist posture and task rotation. Occupational health, if her employer has one, can help.
Broken sleep from the hand plus a week of worry after searching online. Reasoned reassurance and a clear plan help both.

legal.t: If needed, a fit note can say ‘may be fit for work’ with suggested adjustments, such as reduced scanning time or task rotation, rather than time off.
Employers must report carpal tunnel syndrome under RIDDOR 2013 only when the work involves regular use of percussive or vibrating tools. Till scanning does not meet this.

professional.t: Telephone assessment can establish the diagnosis but not thenar wasting or weakness. Arrange a face-to-face examination when motor symptoms are reported, and document the reasoning.
Referring a classic history to neurology reinforces anxiety and uses scarce resources. Explain the diagnosis and the triggers for rethinking.

community.t: Many areas offer direct access to MSK physiotherapy or hand therapy for splints. The British Society for Surgery of the Hand has patient information on carpal tunnel syndrome.

redFlags: Sudden weakness or numbness of the face, arm or leg, speech or vision loss — stroke; 999
Thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction or constant numbness — prompt surgical referral
Bilateral hand and foot symptoms, neck pain with arm symptoms, or other neurological signs — rethink the diagnosis

Broken sleep and a week of worry after searching online
Weight gain, tiredness and feeling cold, put down to age
ice: Idea: “Numbness means MS or a stroke.”
Concern: a serious brain or nerve illness
Expectation: to be told whether it’s MS or a stroke, and to stop being woken at night

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Give the answer first: “This is a typical picture of carpal tunnel syndrome — a nerve squeezed at the wrist. The fingers affected, the night-time pattern and the relief from shaking all point to the wrist, not the brain.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The nerve to your thumb and first fingers runs through a narrow tunnel at the wrist. At night, when your wrist bends, the tunnel narrows and squeezes the nerve — like standing on a hosepipe. Shaking your hand takes your foot off the pipe.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been lying awake thinking this was MS or a stroke. Everything you’ve described points to your wrist instead, and that’s very treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Address the fear directly, with reasons. Offer practical changes for till work and a fit note with adjustments if needed.
sharedPlan: Neutral-position night splint and activity changes (BSSH/GIRFT 2022)
TSH and HbA1c for associations (NICE NG145)
Face-to-face check of thenar bulk and thumb strength; injection, then nerve studies and surgery if persistent or motor signs
safetyNet: 999 for sudden face, arm or leg weakness or numbness, speech or vision loss
Review sooner if numbness spreads, becomes constant, or thumb weakness develops

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by vague or reasonless reassurance, missing the thyroid cue, or ignoring the limits of a telephone consultation. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: ‘It could be a few things — let’s do some tests and see.’
items.why: A classic history deserves a confident, positive diagnosis. Vagueness feeds her fear of MS.
items.fix: “This is a typical picture of carpal tunnel syndrome, and here’s why.”

items.fail: ‘It’s definitely not MS, don’t worry’ — with no explanation.
items.why: Unexplained reassurance doesn’t work with health anxiety. The fear is the reason for the call.
items.fix: Explain the difference: “Stroke is sudden and affects the face, arm or leg; MS lasts days to weeks with other symptoms. Yours follows one nerve at the wrist.”

items.fail: Missing the weight gain, tiredness and cold intolerance.
items.why: Hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of carpal tunnel syndrome (NICE NG145 for testing).
items.fix: Ask about general health and check TSH and HbA1c.

items.why: Thenar wasting or weakness means nerve damage and changes the plan to prompt surgical referral (BSSH/GIRFT 2022).
items.fix: “Because you’re dropping things, I’d like to check your thumb muscles in person this week.”

items.fail: Referring straight to neurology or for nerve conduction studies ‘to be safe’.
items.why: A typical history doesn’t need a nerve study before a splint. Referral reinforces the fear.
items.fix: Start with a night splint, and name exactly what would change the plan.

items.fail: No stroke safety-net because ‘it isn’t a stroke’.
items.why: She fears stroke. Telling her exactly what stroke looks like is both safe and reassuring.
items.fix: “Sudden weakness of your face, arm or leg, slurred speech or loss of vision — call 999. That’s different from what you have.”
